source.title: How Narrative Wrapping Affects LLM Refusal: A Cross-Language Benchmark and Defense
source.authors: Zhan-Kai Ye; Yan-Ning Wang; Yu-Kai Jin; Bo Mei; Fang-Yi Li; Wei Wang; Shang-Qian Gao; Xin Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests a training intervention aimed at carrying refusals through to completion and evaluates refusal behavior, but does not use the original studies’ fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports narrative-wrapping attack rates and representation geometry, plus behavioral outcomes after AXIS training. The wrapping results are not tests of prefilling, suffixes, or decoding changes. The geometry values used to select diagnostic layers or training settings are not included as results unless they directly describe the reported wrapper effect. Cited findings from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper re-implements Qi et al.'s Deep Alignment and the deeper-refusal method DOOR as baselines. It reports their strict refusal rates against narrative-wrapped attacks on three models (Table 2). This is a new-setting result on whether deepening training holds up (V7). The paper's own method, AXIS, is a rotation-plus-DPO defence, not a test of deepening safety beyond the first tokens. Nothing else bears on V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. Additions: AXIS leads the safety–usability composite by a margin that shrinks with scale (+14.5 at 1.7B, +3.0 at 4B, +1.4 at 9B, the last not significant). At 1.7B it is less safe than α-DPO and Booster; its lead there rests on usability. The authors call the representation account correlational, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains LoRA adapters with preference optimization, a representation-rotation objective, and a commitment objective that up-weights early refusal tokens and the terminal token. It does not reproduce the harmful/benign fine-tuning or per-token KL procedures in the named original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model size, rotation dose, seed, attack set, register, and judge. The paper also reports that judge changes can shift refusal scores and that generation length affects measured attack success.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrative wrapping raises attack success from 16–20% bare to 89–96% wrapped on Qwen3-1.7B. It turns the harmful–benign direction 77–86° away from the refusal direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrative wrappers bypass refusal by rotating the harmful–benign representation contrast off the refusal direction, largely independent of register.

fits_no_version.finding: A lenient pipeline judge reports 28.8–45.1% wrapped attack success where the strict judge reports 89.4–95.7%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured jailbreak success depends heavily on how warn-then-answer responses are judged.

fits_no_version.finding: AXIS (DPO + rotation + commitment) raises strict refusal on wrapped attacks: 71.9/68.1 at 1.7B, 94.6/98.8 at 4B, 98.8/99.3 at 9B. The rotation term drives held-out-wrapper gains, and removing DPO causes 27–41% benign over-refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training harmful-request representations back onto the refusal direction restores refusal under unseen narrative wrappers.

record.problems: The representation account is correlational and population-level and does not predict individual wrapped-request refusals. AXIS uses one shared rotation dose across models; the 1.7B dose preference did not reproduce across training runs. The 4B replication has two seeds and the 9B replication one seed. Headline rates rely on one vendor’s judge, and the authors report judge drift and uneven guard-model agreement. Human annotation does not cover the 4B and 9B arms.
record.rows_left_out: Not all per-seed ablation values, external-method results, dose sweeps, and case-study responses are recorded. The retained rows prioritize the wrapper results and the AXIS training outcomes directly relevant to V7; additional results appear in Tables 2–4, 12–15 and Appendix O.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Only narrative/role-play wrappers. No prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes.
No localisation of safety in weights or ranks.
No test of why alignment is shallow.

Prefill attacks are not tested. Robustness of Deep Alignment to subsequent fine-tuning is not tested. Per-position safety after deepening is not measured. Deep Alignment and DOOR are only evaluated against narrative wrappers, at the authors' coefficients and without re-tuning, with 195 updates vs 417 for the main arms.

missing.what: Deep Alignment (Qi et al. 2025 deepening objective) strict refusal on harm334/ood834 and over-refusal/helpfulness on xstest for 1.7B, 4B and 9B; base values for comparison.
DOOR (deeper-refusal, Zhao et al. 2025b) strict refusal and over-refusal on all three models, including the 92 empty 9B responses.
Human-labelled case study: Deep Alignment and DOOR give direct answers to wrapped attacks hb_0112 and srf_0095 at 1.7B.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked AXIS rows to V7, but AXIS is not a deepening method. The study's actual V7 evidence is the re-implemented Deep Alignment and DOOR baselines, which no row records. Caveats on those baselines: run at authors' coefficients with 195 updates vs 417 for the main arms. Deep Alignment's loss is dominated by long helpful targets (23:1 tokens). Results are seed 0 in a single judging batch with one vendor's judge.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning experiment testing whether a few to a few hundred examples remove safety.
No ordinary or carefully chosen benign-data fine-tuning experiment testing erosion of safety.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models, or measurement of how KL varies over response positions.
The paper tests narrative wrappers, not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
LoRA is used as a training implementation, but the paper does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
The paper does not test whether data or an objective causes the claimed first-token concentration or shallowness.
Tests a commitment objective that reinforces a refusal through its end, but does not measure whether safety is distributed beyond the first tokens or whether it survives subsequent fine-tuning.

relationships.condition: Deep Alignment (Qi et al. 2025) on Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B and GLM-4-9B, narrative-wrapped attacks (harm334, ood834)
relationships.reason: Text-based (no rows; see missing). Strict refusal rises only partly: 5.4→24.6 and 29.1→57.9 at 1.7B; 5.1→42.2 and 54.4→71.6 at 4B; 7.5→37.4 and 38.0→73.9 at 9B (Table 2). Most wrapped attacks still succeed in distribution.
relationships.display_finding: Strict refusal rose only partly, from 5.4 to 24.6 and 29.1 to 57.9 at 1.7B, 5.1 to 42.2 and 54.4 to 71.6 at 4B, and 7.5 to 37.4 and 38.0 to 73.9 at 9B.

source_check.condition: Deep Alignment (Qi et al. 2025) on Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B and GLM-4-9B, narrative-wrapped attacks (harm334, ood834)
source_check.reason: Protection is incomplete on all three models. The verdict explanation swaps the larger models' trained results. Table 2 gives harm334/ood834 refusal rates: Qwen3-1.7B 24.6%/57.9%, Qwen3-4B 37.4%/73.9%, GLM-4-9B 42.2%/71.6%; respective baselines are 5.4%/29.1%, 5.1%/54.4%, and 7.5%/38.0%.

relationships.reason: Text-based (no rows). DOOR barely changes refusal at 1.7B: harm 10.2 vs base 5.4, ood 32.7 vs 29.1 (Table 2).
relationships.display_finding: DOOR barely changed refusal at 1.7B, 10.2 versus 5.4 on harm334 and 32.7 versus 29.1 on ood834.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Table 2 reports small gains: harm334 refusal 5.4%→10.2% and ood834 refusal 29.1%→32.7%. This is incomplete protection rather than an absent or reversed effect.

relationships.reason: Text-based (no rows). DOOR reaches 94.3/87.1 (97.8 excluding 92 empty responses) at 4B and 95.7/97.8 at 9B, against base 5.1/54.4 and 7.5/38.0 (Table 2; Appendix H).
relationships.display_finding: Strict refusal reached 94.3 and 87.1 at 4B (97.8 when 92 empty responses are excluded) and 95.7 and 97.8 at 9B, against base rates of 5.1 and 54.4 and of 7.5 and 38.0.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Strong protection supports V7, but the explanation misattributes the numbers. Table 2 gives Qwen3-4B harm334/ood834 refusal 93.7%/95.7%, versus baseline 5.1%/54.4%; GLM-4-9B gives 94.3%/87.1%, versus 7.5%/38.0%. The 9B ood834 rate becomes 97.8% after excluding 92 empty responses (Table 2 footnote; Appendix H).

tranche.reason: Re-implemented deepening methods are tested against narrative-wrapped attacks, including held-out wrapper genres: a new setting bearing on V7.

source_check.notes: Verdict labels pass; numerical explanations for l0 and l2 need correction. Baselines use published settings without benchmark retuning; DOOR and Deep Alignment receive 195 updates versus 417 for the main AXIS arms.

statements.correction: This study reports incomplete protection from Deep Alignment and small refusal gains from DOOR on Qwen3-1.7B. The statement's numerical results concern other studies.

reader_labels.reason: Training with the full method raises refusal on held-out wrappers to 98.8% and 99.3% on the larger models, and yields improved refusal across registers on Qwen3-1.7B (r18–r19, r23–r28).

reader_labels.reason: The refusal improvements are incomplete on Qwen3-1.7B, with 68.1% on held-out wrappers and 71.9% in distribution; the paper also reports seed variability and dose sensitivity (r15–r16, r22).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Preference-only training does not improve held-out-wrapper refusal in the reported ablation, while adding rotation helps but remains below the full AXIS result (r20–r22).
